title: Strain- and potential-controlled tunneling in monolayer MoS$_2$
authors: Hasna Chnafa, Rachid El Aitouni, Clarence Cortes, David Laroze, Ahmed Jellal
abstract: We present a theoretical study of spin- and valley-resolved quantum transport in monolayer MoS$_2$ under the combined influence of mechanical strain and an external scalar potential, a combination whose simultaneous unexplored. Within an effective massive Dirac Hamiltonian that incorporates intrinsic spin--orbit coupling, strain induces valley-dependent momentum shifts that lift the degeneracy between the $K$ and $K'$ valleys and strongly modify the transport characteristics. The scalar potential modifies the tunneling spectrum, leading to pronounced changes in resonant transmission, Fabry--Pérot interference, and conductance. We show that the interplay between strain and electrostatic potential enables efficient control of both valley and spin polarization of the transmitted current. In particular, we identify a dual-knob control scheme in which the barrier width governs the frequency of conductance oscillations while strain independently controls their phase and amplitude. Furthermore, we predict electrostatic spin inversion -- a sign reversal of spin polarization achievable purely by gate tuning at finite strain, requiring no geometric reconfiguration. Depending on the strain orientation, the transmission probability and conductance can be selectively suppressed or enhanced, resulting in highly tunable valley- and spin-polarized transport. These findings demonstrate that strain and potential engineering provide orthogonal and independently operable mechanisms for controlling conductance as well as spin and valley degrees of freedom in monolayer MoS$_2$, offering promising prospects for spintronic and valleytronic device applications.
summary: This theoretical study details how combining mechanical strain and electrostatic gating can independently control spin and valley polarization in monolayer MoS2. By analyzing quantum transport through potential barriers, the authors reveal a powerful 'dual-knob' mechanism for tuning conductance resonances and predict novel effects like gate-tunable spin inversion.
main_problem: The study investigates spin- and valley-resolved quantum transport in monolayer MoS2 when subjected to the simultaneous influence of mechanical strain and an external scalar potential.
main_result: The interplay between strain and potential allows for independent, orthogonal control over both valley and spin polarization. Specifically, they predict a dual-knob control scheme and demonstrate electrostatic spin inversion purely via gate tuning at finite strain.
method: The authors employed theoretical modeling using an effective massive Dirac Hamiltonian incorporating intrinsic spin-orbit coupling to calculate electron transmission coefficients by matching boundary conditions across potential barriers.
model_or_system: The system is monolayer MoS2, modeled using a k.p approach with an effective Hamiltonian that includes terms for strain (acting as a gauge field) and an external electrostatic barrier potential. The transport is analyzed in the presence of valley (K/K') and spin degrees of freedom.
key_observables: Spin polarization ($P_s$), valley polarization ($P_v$), conductance, and Fabry-Pérot resonance characteristics.
important_parameters: Mechanical strain ($\epsilon$), barrier width ($L$), incident energy ($E$), and the strength of the potential ($V_0$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes a continuum effective Dirac Hamiltonian, neglects disorder effects (like impurity scattering), and treats the barriers as perfectly sharp rectangular profiles.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic setups showing strain/potential application; results show how transmission probability ($T$) exhibits resonances whose frequency is controlled by $L$ and whose phase/amplitude are independently tuned by $\epsilon$.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework using a modified Dirac Hamiltonian, derives the coupled differential equations for transport across a barrier, calculates transmission coefficients via boundary matching, and finally analyzes how varying strain and potential allows for independent control over spin and valley polarization.
why_interesting: This work demonstrates advanced quantum engineering principles—using external fields (strain/potential) to manipulate fundamental symmetries (spin/valley)—which is highly relevant to designing next-generation spintronic and valleytronic devices.
